1. Preservation of Cultural and Social Homogeneity

  • Democratic Compatibility: Proponents argued that immigrants from countries with democratic traditions (like Great Britain or Scandinavia) were better prepared for American self-governance.
  • Language and Religion: Groups that were Protestant and English-speaking were viewed as easier to integrate into the existing social fabric, whereas Catholic, Jewish, and non-Christian immigrants were viewed with skepticism by the Protestant majority of the time.

3. Economic Protection and Labor Stability

Economic concerns were a significant driver for restrictive quotas. Labor unions and some economic theorists argued that an influx of low-skilled labor from restricted regions created negative outcomes for domestic workers:

  • Wage Suppression: Critics of unrestricted immigration argued that a surplus of foreign labor allowed corporations to keep wages low and working conditions poor.
  • Standard of Living: It was argued that by limiting immigration, the government could protect the "American standard of living" and ensure that the labor market remained tight enough to favor resident workers.

4. Influence of Eugenics and "Scientific Racism"

In the early 20th century, the eugenics movement was highly influential among American academics and policymakers.

  • Intellectual Hierarchy: Many proponents of the 1924 Act relied on the "science" of the day, which falsely claimed there was a biological hierarchy of races and ethnicities. They argued that certain "Nordic" or "Alpine" races were intellectually and morally superior to "Mediterranean" or "Semitic" groups.
  • Racial Purity: Eugenics advocates argued that "interbreeding" between Northern Europeans and other groups would lead to "racial degeneration" and weaken the national character.

The period following World War I and the Russian Revolution saw a rise in "Nativism" fueled by fears of radicalism.
